name: Expected value
purpose: Finds the long-run average outcome when different outcomes have different probabilities.
realWorld: Used for expected investment return, expected derivative payoff, credit loss, insurance loss and decisions under uncertainty.
plainEnglish: Multiply each outcome by its probability, then add.
whyItWorks: Imagine the same uncertain situation happens 100 times.
A 30% outcome is expected about 30 times; a 70% outcome is expected about 70 times.
Total payoff over 100 repetitions is 30 × first payoff + 70 × second payoff.
Divide by 100 to get the ordinary arithmetic mean.
This simplifies to 0.30 × first payoff + 0.70 × second payoff. That is why probabilities are the weights.
Therefore E(X) is a probability-weighted mean, not a simple average unless all outcomes are equally likely.

name: Operational risk capital approaches
purpose: The three regulatory approaches for calculating how much capital a bank must hold against operational risk.
realWorld: Determines a bank's Basel operational-risk capital charge — a heavily tested regulatory topic.
whyItWorks: Basic indicator approach: capital charge is measured firmwide as a percentage of average annual gross income — the simplest, least risk-sensitive method.

name: Loss frequency and loss severity
purpose: The two independent dimensions used to model operational risk losses.
realWorld: Operational risk models combine a frequency distribution with a severity distribution to estimate total expected/unexpected loss.

name: Hypothesis testing framework
purpose: The structure of a statistical hypothesis test: null vs. alternative hypothesis, and one-tailed vs. two-tailed tests.
realWorld: The framework underlying every test statistic on the exam (t-test, chi-squared test, F-test).

purpose: The requirement that a time series' mean, variance, and autocovariances stay stable over time for AR models to be valid.
realWorld: A prerequisite check before fitting an AR(1) or similar autoregressive time-series model.
whyItWorks: A time series is covariance stationary if its mean, variance, and covariances with lagged/leading values are all stable over time.
Covariance stationarity is a requirement for meaningfully using autoregressive (AR) models — see [[ar1-process]].

Models fit to a series that lacks covariance stationarity are unstable and don't produce meaningful forecasts, since the statistical relationships the model relies on are themselves changing over time.
trap: Covariance stationarity is a precondition to CHECK before trusting an AR(1) forecast — a non-stationary series can produce an AR fit that looks reasonable but forecasts poorly.
memoryHook: Stable mean, stable variance, stable relationships over time = good AR candidate.

questions.prompt: Why would fitting an AR(1) model to a non-stationary time series produce unreliable forecasts?
questions.answer: Because the model assumes the statistical relationships (mean, variance, autocovariance) are constant over time, and a non-stationary series violates that assumption — the fitted coefficients don't reliably describe future behavior.
questions.hint: Think about what an AR(1) coefficient Φ is implicitly assuming stays constant.
questions.explanation: AR(1) and similar models rely on covariance stationarity; fitting them to a non-stationary series produces unstable, unreliable forecasts because the underlying relationships are shifting.

name: Seasonality in time series
purpose: A repeating pattern in a time series that recurs at the same point each year (or other fixed cycle).
realWorld: Needed to correctly model time series like retail sales or energy demand that have predictable within-year swings.
whyItWorks: Seasonality is a pattern in a time series that tends to repeat from year to year (or other regular period).
Approach 1: regression analysis with seasonal dummy variables — one dummy variable per season/period, isolating each period's typical deviation from trend.
Approach 2: seasonal differencing — subtracting the value from the same period one cycle ago to remove the repeating pattern.
A trend can be combined with seasonal dummy variables in a single model to capture both the long-run direction and the within-year pattern simultaneously.
trap: Ignoring seasonality and fitting only a trend line to a seasonal series will produce systematically biased forecasts at certain times of year — the residuals will show an obvious repeating pattern if seasonality is missed.
memoryHook: A pattern that repeats every cycle, not just noise.

questions.explanation: Seasonal dummy variables explicitly model each period's typical deviation, while seasonal differencing removes the repeating pattern by comparing each observation to the same point in the prior cycle.

name: Swap credit risk
purpose: Because a swap is a zero-sum contract, whenever one counterparty's position has positive value, the other's is exactly negative.
realWorld: Explains why only one side of an interest rate or currency swap bears counterparty credit risk at any given time.
whyItWorks: Vswap(A) + Vswap(B) = 0 always holds for the two counterparties of the same swap — the contract is a zero-sum transfer of value between them.
Whenever one side's value is positive, the other side's value must be negative by the same amount — e.g., if Vswap(A) > 0, then Vswap(B) < 0.
If a swap has a positive value to one counterparty, that party is exposed to credit risk on the other — if the counterparty defaults, the party with the positive-value position loses that value.
trap: Only the counterparty holding the positive-value side bears meaningful default-driven loss — the party with negative value has no economic loss exposure from the other's default (ignoring termination mechanics).
memoryHook: One side's gain is exactly the other side's loss.

name: Historical simulation VaR
purpose: Computing VaR directly from a sample of actual historical returns, without assuming any particular distribution.
realWorld: A widely used, model-free alternative to delta-normal VaR that doesn't require assuming returns are normally distributed.
whyItWorks: Historical simulation VaR uses actual historical return data rather than assuming a specific distribution (like the normal distribution used in delta-normal VaR).
Procedure: accumulate a number of past daily (or periodic) returns, rank them from highest to lowest, and identify the appropriate lowest percentile of returns.
For example, to compute a 5% daily VaR, you would identify the return at the 5th percentile of the ranked historical distribution.

Because it makes no distributional assumption, historical simulation VaR naturally captures fat tails and skewness that delta-normal VaR would miss — but it is entirely dependent on the historical window used.
trap: Historical simulation VaR's accuracy is fully dependent on the historical sample used — if the lookback window didn't include a crisis, the method won't 'know' extreme moves are possible.
memoryHook: Rank actual past returns; the cutoff percentile IS your VaR.

questions.prompt: Why might historical simulation VaR fail to capture the risk of an unprecedented market crash?
questions.answer: Because it only uses returns that have actually occurred in the historical sample window — if the lookback period never included an extreme event, the ranked historical distribution won't include one either.
questions.hint: Think about what data the method is fundamentally built from.
questions.explanation: Historical simulation VaR is only as good as its historical sample — a crash outside the sample window simply won't appear in the ranked distribution used to compute VaR.

name: Central counterparties (CCPs)
purpose: When trades are centrally cleared, a CCP steps in as the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer.
realWorld: Central to understanding post-2008 derivatives market structure reforms and their tradeoffs.
whyItWorks: When trades are centrally cleared, a CCP becomes the seller to every buyer and the buyer to every seller — this replaces bilateral counterparty exposure with exposure to the CCP itself.
Advantages of CCPs: loss mutualization (losses are shared across members), legal and operational efficiency, liquidity, standardized documentation, and increased transparency.
Disadvantages of CCPs: moral hazard, adverse selection, procyclicality, and concentrated credit risk in the CCP itself.

Risks faced by CCPs: default risk, model risk, liquidity risk, operational risk, legal risk, and investment risk — default of a clearing member (and the ripple effects through the system) is generally considered the most significant risk a CCP faces.
trap: Central clearing doesn't eliminate counterparty risk — it concentrates it in the CCP, which is why CCP default risk and its 'default waterfall' resources are themselves a heavily scrutinized systemic risk.
memoryHook: CCP = buyer to every seller, seller to every buyer.

name: Bonds with embedded options
purpose: Callable and putable bonds give one side the right to force early redemption, which changes how their prices behave versus yields.
realWorld: Explains why callable/putable bond price-yield curves deviate from an option-free bond's curve, especially the negative convexity of callable bonds.
whyItWorks: A callable bond gives the issuer the right to buy back the bond in the future at a set price — as yields fall, the bond is increasingly likely to be called, so its price rises at a decreasing rate: negative convexity.
A putable bond gives the bondholder the right to sell the bond back to the issuer at a set price — this protects the holder from large price declines as yields rise.

Callable bonds are priced lower than an equivalent option-free bond (issuer's option has value to the issuer); putable bonds are priced higher than an equivalent option-free bond (holder's option has value to the holder).
trap: Negative convexity specifically describes callable bonds near/below the call price — don't assume all embedded-option bonds share the same convexity behavior; putable bonds retain positive convexity.
memoryHook: Callable = issuer's option = price capped, negative convexity. Putable = holder's option = downside protected.

questions.explanation: As yields fall, the likelihood of the issuer calling the bond rises, capping upside price appreciation and producing the negative convexity characteristic of callable bonds.

name: Portfolio insurance
purpose: Combining an underlying portfolio with long put options to protect against a decline in market value.
realWorld: A classic downside-protection strategy, and one whose dynamic (synthetic) form contributed to the 1987 market crash.
whyItWorks: Portfolio insurance combines (1) an underlying position or portfolio with (2) long put options that protect the underlying investment from a decline in market value.

name: Exercising American options early
purpose: The rules governing when it is ever rational to exercise an American option before its expiration date.
realWorld: A frequently tested nuance distinguishing American from European options — early exercise is often NOT optimal even though American options technically allow it.
whyItWorks: It is never optimal to exercise an American call early on a non-dividend-paying stock — you always do at least as well selling the call as exercising it, since the call retains time value.

name: Option-adjusted spread (OAS)
purpose: The spread over the benchmark curve after removing (adjusting for) the effect of any embedded optionality in the bond's cash flows.

name: Financial Crisis of 2007-2009: contributing factors
purpose: The three widely cited structural factors that contributed to the 2007-2009 global financial crisis.
realWorld: A frequently tested case study explaining the systemic mechanics behind the crisis, distinct from any single firm's individual failure.
whyItWorks: Factor 1: banks relaxed their lending standards, moving to an originate-to-distribute model that increased subprime lending, since originators no longer bore the full risk of loans they made.
Factor 2: institutions increasingly funded themselves using short-term facilities, which increased their liquidity risk when short-term funding markets seized up.
Factor 3: the Lehman Brothers default caused a broad loss of confidence, with banks refusing to lend to each other, ultimately requiring central banks to step in and provide liquidity support.
trap: The originate-to-distribute model is the structural link between 'relaxed lending standards' and 'the crisis spreading widely' — because loans were resold via CDOs (see [[credit-derivatives]]), the risk of bad underwriting was distributed system-wide instead of staying with the originator.
memoryHook: Loose lending -> short-term funding -> Lehman default -> frozen interbank lending.

questions.prompt: How did the 'originate-to-distribute' model contribute to the spread of risk during the 2007-2009 financial crisis?
questions.answer: Because originators sold off the loans they made (often repackaged into CDOs) rather than holding them, they had less incentive to maintain strict underwriting standards, and the resulting risk spread widely across the financial system to whoever held the repackaged securities.
questions.hint: Think about how loan originators' incentives changed once they no longer had to hold the loans themselves.
questions.explanation: The originate-to-distribute model weakened underwriting discipline and spread mortgage credit risk broadly across the system via securitization, amplifying the crisis's reach.
